opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. That's a question I think about a lot, because clinical gestalt is very real. When an experienced oncologist or radiologist walks into a room or looks at a scan, they're integrating a huge amount of information almost instantly. They notice how the patient looks, how they're moving, what the family is saying, the subtle texture of an image. A lot of that never makes it into the chart in any structured way. It comes from years of pattern recognition, and it's often remarkably accurate.

I don't see AI as a replacement for that. What these models do well is pick up patterns humans can't easily perceive or quantify. In my own work with medical imaging, we've seen that there's information in a CT scan, in the heterogeneity of a tumor for example, that relates to outcomes, and the human eye just isn't built to extract it reliably. So the model sees things the clinician can't, and the clinician sees things the model never will, because the model only knows what's in the data we gave it.

The interesting part is where the two disagree. If a model flags a patient as high risk and the clinician's gut says they're doing fine, that's a moment worth paying attention to. Sometimes the clinician is picking up on context the model is missing. Sometimes the model is seeing something early that hasn't shown up clinically yet. The goal should be tools that support that conversation, not tools that override judgment or that people blindly defer to.

There's also an equity piece. Gestalt is shaped by experience, which means it can carry biases, and so can models trained on historical data. Neither is neutral. So I think the best path is pairing them thoughtfully, being transparent about what each one is based on, and keeping the clinician and the patient at the center of the decision.

r001.rationale: The response says clinicians notice how patients look and move and what family members say, and that much of this information never enters the structured chart.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention a study comparing radiologists with AI on predicting two-year survival for pancreatic cancer patients.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So, clinician gestalt is one of those things that sounds almost mystical when you first hear it, but it's actually quite concrete when you unpack it. An experienced surgeon walks into a room, looks at a patient, and within a few seconds has a sense of "this person is sick" or "this person is going to do badly after surgery." They often can't fully articulate why. It's pattern recognition built up over thousands of encounters, integrating things that never make it into the chart. How the patient is sitting, their skin color, whether they make eye contact, how they walked in from the waiting room, what their family member's face looks like.

And what's striking is that when you actually study it, gestalt holds up remarkably well. In a lot of prognostic tasks, a seasoned clinician's gut call is as good as or better than our formal risk scores. That should be humbling for people like me who build models.

But I think the right framing isn't gestalt versus AI. They're seeing different parts of the picture. Gestalt is extraordinary at integrating messy, multimodal, in-the-room information, but it's inconsistent. It depends on who's on shift, how tired they are, what their last few patients looked like. It's also hard to teach and hard to transfer. A model, on the other hand, is tireless and consistent, and it can look at things a human simply can't perceive. In my work, that's things like subtle texture features in a CT scan, body composition quantified across hundreds of slices, patterns across thousands of patients that no single clinician will ever have in their head.

Where I think we've gone wrong historically is treating this as a competition, building a model, showing it beats the clinician on some metric, and declaring victory. Clinicians rightly push back on that, because they know the model never saw the patient. The more interesting question for me is: what does the model know that the clinician doesn't, and vice versa, and how do you put those together? When we've looked at combining imaging-derived features with clinical judgment, the combination tends to outperform either alone.

The other thing I'd say is that gestalt has blind spots we should be honest about. It encodes bias. It's shaped by who the clinician trained with and which patients they've seen. And it degrades in situations that are rare or novel, where there's no pattern to recognize. That's exactly where a well-built model can help, as long as we're equally honest that models encode the biases of their training data too.

So my view is that AI's job isn't to replace the gestalt, it's to make it more reliable. Give the clinician a second signal, show them the cases where their instinct and the model disagree, and treat those disagreements as the most informative moments in the whole workflow. That's where the learning happens, for the human and for the model.

r001.rationale: The response says clinicians integrate in-room visual cues absent from the chart, including posture, skin color, eye contact, and how a patient walks.

r002.rationale: It makes a general claim about experienced clinicians’ prognostic judgments but does not mention the pancreatic cancer study, the two most experienced radiologists, or predicting survival beyond two years.

astra-6.text:
I think clinicians’ gestalt is an ability to bring together lots of different signals. You look at a patient, you listen to them, you draw on your experience, and you form an impression that may be difficult to articulate. That’s valuable, and it’s not necessarily captured in the data we give an AI system.

AI can complement that by identifying patterns that are difficult for us to see or quantify. But it only sees what we provide it. A model working from an image doesn’t have the whole patient in front of it. So I see the opportunity as bringing those perspectives together: using AI to give clinicians additional information while keeping their judgment and the patient’s context central.

sol-6.1.text:
I think clinicians’ gestalt captures something important: they’re bringing together experience, subtle cues, and the context of the person in front of them. Some of that information may never make it into the medical record, so an AI system may not have access to it.

But clinical intuition can also be biased, and AI can help identify patterns that are difficult for us to see. I see the opportunity as combining those strengths. When the clinician and the model disagree, that should prompt a closer look: what is each picking up on, and what might each be missing?
